cim: The future of underwriting: Integrating digital evidence, artificial intelligence and human judgment
cim_eredeti: The future of underwriting: Integrating digital evidence, artificial intelligence and human judgment
szoveg_eredeti:
Underwriting is entering a new phase of maturity. The industry is moving beyond experimentation with accelerated underwriting and digital health data and toward a more integrated model built on disciplined risk assessment, scalable underwriting workflows, and robust monitoring. Artificial intelligence remains much earlier in its evolution, but will likely become a key differentiator for carriers that can identify practical use cases, govern them effectively, and translate them into measurable underwriting value.

Munich Re Life US’s 2026 Underwriting Survey reflects underwriting practices reported by 30 participating U.S. individual life insurers as of January 2026. This survey represents an evolution of Munich Re’s long-running Accelerated Underwriting Survey, which has been conducted biennially since 2018. While accelerated underwriting remained a central focus, this year’s survey broadened the scope to capture a more comprehensive view of underwriting modernization. This paper highlights selected high-level themes, while the detailed survey results and benchmarking opportunities are reserved exclusively for survey participants.

The research provides a broad view of how underwriting practices are evolving as carriers seek to improve speed and customer experience while maintaining mortality protection and operational control. Across the findings, one message is clear: the next generation of underwriting will not be defined by a single technology. Competitive advantage will come from how effectively insurers connect data, decisioning, workflow, and artificial intelligence with human expertise.

Four key trends shaping the life insurance industry

Accelerated underwriting has become a core operating model, with attention shifting from adoption to optimization.

Digital health data is changing how evidence is selected, combined, and interpreted. Electronic health records are moving from emerging input to essential infrastructure, but usability remains a constraint.

Traditional underwriting requirements are becoming more targeted and data-informed, not obsolete.

Artificial intelligence (AI) adoption is advancing, but inconsistently across underwriting programs. AI is creating value first as a productivity and decision-support tool for underwriters.

For the purposes of the survey, "accelerated underwriting" – or AUW – is defined as the waiving of traditional underwriting requirements (e.g., fluids, medical exams) for a subset of applicants that meet favorable risk requirements in an otherwise "fully underwritten" – or FUW – life insurance process. AUW can also apply to processes that don’t have a FUW alternative path, thereby waiving traditional requirements on all applicants and automatically declining those that don’t meet the AUW risk requirements. Simplified issue and guaranteed issue programs were not in scope.

One of the clearest signals from the survey is this: AUW is no longer “new,” as all but one of the survey participants reported having an AUW program in production as of January 2026. Nearly all carriers have implemented AUW pathways, and the conversation has shifted. With accelerated programs now widely established, carriers are focusing on the next challenge: expanding acceleration while preserving mortality performance.

Accelerated underwriting has moved from a differentiated innovation to a foundational capability in the U.S. individual life market. As adoption has broadened, carrier priorities have evolved. Program leaders are increasingly focused on expanding access thoughtfully, improving underwriting evidence strategies, strengthening monitoring, and directing underwriter attention to the cases where judgment creates the most value.

AUW eligibility by face amount has continued to broaden since the original AUW Survey in 2018, but widening the front door is only one measure of progress. Sustainable performance depends on what happens after an applicant enters the accelerated pathway: how evidence is ordered, how exceptions are managed, and how many applicants ultimately receive an accelerated offer. Acceleration rates (as a percentage of eligible applicants) have plateaued in recent years and continue to be a challenge for the industry. See Figure 1 for details on eligibility and acceleration trends.

Another survey finding is that accelerated underwriting does not necessarily mean fully automated underwriting. Human underwriter review remains prevalent in the majority of accelerated cases, particularly when applicants approach program eligibility boundaries or digital evidence introduces complexity that signals a need for additional underwriter or clinical interpretation. The strongest operating models use technology to streamline routine applications while preserving human judgment for nuanced cases. The next phase of AUW progress may therefore depend less on simply expanding eligibility and more on improving evidence usability and data optimization in underwriting workflows.

Underwriting tools and data source usage remain a key focus of the 2026 Underwriting Survey. The results highlight how AUW has shifted from simply waiving fluids to orchestrating multiple evidence sources to determine which applicants can proceed without traditional requirements. Mature AUW programs often rely on a layered data strategy: some tools are used broadly and routinely to screen applicants, while others are deployed selectively when age, amount, risk indicators, or prior findings suggest that additional evidence is needed.

Given the importance of understanding how and why evidence is ordered, the survey continued to capture how underwriting tools and information sources are being used to triage or classify risks in the accelerated pipeline (i.e., routine or selective usage, evaluating, or not using). In this year’s survey, “selective” usage was differentiated into specific reasons, including age and amount requirements (AAR), for-cause requests, and other reasons. While the staple AUW tools – Medical Information Bureau (MIB), prescription history (Rx), and motor vehicle records (MVR) – continue to be used routinely by the vast majority of carriers, newer digital health data – medical claims data (Dx), clinical labs, and electronic health records (EHRs) – is now also used by a large majority of carriers, primarily on a selective basis and for varying reasons. While lab data is most commonly used as an AAR, EHRs are more likely to be requested for-cause in AUW decisioning. When evaluating aggregate usage trends (routine and selective) over time, the steepest growth continues to be seen in the newer digital health data sources – medical claims, clinical labs, and EHRs – as detailed in Figure 2. For visual clarity, Figure 2 highlights three benchmark years - 2018, 2022, and 2026 - while the accompanying discussion draws on the full survey history.

Modern underwriting increasingly relies on a layered evidence ecosystem. Application data, MIB information, motor vehicle reports, prescription history, medical claims, laboratory data, EHRs, and financial data each contribute different underwriting evidence. The strategic challenge is to determine which sources to use, when to use them and how to translate them into consistent underwriting action.

Digital health data can strengthen risk assessment by revealing clinical history, treatment patterns, and potential nondisclosures that may not be evident from application data alone. At the same time, richer evidence can surface complexity that appropriately leads to additional review. The value of digital data should therefore be measured not only by speed or straight-through processing, but also by the quality and confidence of the resulting underwriting decision, which can be monitored through pre- and post-issue auditing practices.
